Phase III – High-Flow Validation: Full-scale operation was demonstrated at SwRI’s MRF to identify limits of plasma stability under realistic gas velocities and pressures. 4. Phase IV – Engine Integration and Demonstration: The reformer was installed on a Cooper AJAX 2802 ULE engine and later on a Cummins X15N research engine to evaluate methane leak reductions and combustion effects under field-representative conditions. 2.3.2 System Overview The integrated system (Figure 1) consists of three primary subsystems: 1. Power-Electronics Control Module – generates pulsed high-voltage discharges with peak amplitudes up to 20 kV and average power under 4 kW. 2. Plasma Reformer Module – houses concentric-electrode reaction zones within an 8-inch- diameter pressure vessel. Tangential gas injection and a defined flow path create a swirl flow that stabilizes the plasma and increases residence time. 3. Engine Integration Loop – connects the reformer outlet directly to the engine fuel line, allowing reformed fuel (CH + H + C H ) to enter the cylinders and enhance combustion 4 2 x y efficiency. 2.3.3 Design and Modeling CFD simulations were performed using steady-state Navier–Stokes equations with species transport models to evaluate gas-velocity fields and pressure loss through the plasma reformer. The analysis guided optimization of internal geometry, swirl flow, and chamber diameter to ensure efficient plasma-gas interaction while maintaining minimal pressure drop. The concept design used for CFD modeling is shown in Figure 2, which illustrates the cylindrical configuration with a Southwest Research Institute® U.S. DOE Award Number DE-FE0032301 Public Version - 3 - DE-FE0032301 Final Report swirl-inducing inlet section that passes over an annulus electrode region. The reformer’s annular and concentric electrode geometry provided uniform discharge spacing and adequate gas residence time within the plasma region. Flow-field visualization from the CFD model (Figure 3) demonstrates the velocity distribution and mixing characteristics across the plasma zone. The color contours and streamlines highlight the formation of a central recirculation region generated by the swirl inlets, which promotes stable plasma behavior at elevated flow rates. A two- dimensional cross-section of the flow domain (Figure 4) was used to quantify velocity magnitude along the reformer axis. At smaller internal diameters (1 inch), local gas velocities approached 160 m/s, confirming the need to enlarge the flow passage to maintain suitable residence time for plasma-induced reactions. Parametric simulations examining the relationship between pipe diameter and total pressure loss are summarized in Figure 5. The results show that pressure losses decrease rapidly with increasing diameter, reaching the design target of less than one percent of inlet pressure when the diameter exceeds approximately 2.5 inches. This criterion was used to define the final 8-inch-diameter housing selected for fabrication. Figure 2 intentionally omitted from public version. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) modeling was used to inform the conceptual design of the plasma reformer and evaluate gas flow behavior within the reaction zone. The simulations supported selection of an internal flow configuration that promotes uniform gas distribution, adequate residence time, and stable plasma interaction while maintaining low pressure loss.
